name: How We Learned to Feed Billions
description: Ploughs, canals, fertiliser and new crops: the farming and food inventions that let a few million hunters become eight billion people.

checkpoints.name: First fields and waterworks
checkpoints.note: Early farmers ploughed, dug canals and flooded rice fields in Mesopotamia, Egypt, India and China. Qanats carried groundwater through tunnels, shadufs, norias and screws lifted water, and fish and bees were farmed.

checkpoints.name: Harnesses, wheels and chinampas
checkpoints.note: Horse collars let horses pull ploughs, and Aztec farmers built chinampas, raised fields of lake mud often called floating gardens. Farmers across Asia, Africa and Europe learned to feed growing towns.

checkpoints.name: Machines and cans
checkpoints.note: Seed drills, cotton gins and combine harvesters saved labour. Canning, pasteurisation and margarine changed what ended up on a dinner table, and barbed wire fenced the plains.

checkpoints.name: Fertiliser and pesticide
checkpoints.note: The Haber process made fertiliser from air, tractors replaced horses, refrigerators changed the kitchen, and DDT and other chemicals fought crop pests.

checkpoints.name: The Green Revolution and after
checkpoints.note: Short-stalked wheat and rice spared much of India and Mexico from famine. Later came concern about pesticides, the first modified crops, and new ways to grow food indoors.
